prompt: Your client owns a business-district hotel in Mumbai with a single uniform room rate. Management is considering raising the room rate from $160 to $180 a night to lift profits, and wants your recommendation on whether to do it.

clarifying.answer: There is no special trigger; management is simply exploring a price increase as one lever to raise profits.
All rooms are similar and carry the same uniform rate; $160 is the actual rate, not an average.
About 80% are business travellers and 20% are tourists.
Business guests bill their company; companies also cover extras. Employees may stay anywhere priced under a $220-per-night cap, with no cap on extras.
One nearby hotel charges about $160, but the client has a stronger business centre that corporate guests rely on for meetings.

facts.note: Business guests are effectively price-inelastic up to the $220 corporate cap and are anchored by the business centre; tourists pay out of pocket and are price-elastic.

exhibits.title: Customer Mix and Corporate Travel Policy
exhibits.unlock_condition: Candidate asks who the customers are and how price-sensitive each type is, or asks to segment demand before judging the price move.
exhibits.so_what: 80% of guests are business travellers who are insensitive to the rate up to a $220 cap and are anchored by the business centre. Only the 20% tourist segment is genuinely price-elastic.

phases.name: opening
phases.interviewer_instructions: State the prompt. Do not volunteer the customer mix or the corporate cap. Wait for the candidate to restate the decision and begin clarifying.

coaching.explain: A pricing decision hinges on customer price elasticity. A strong candidate restates the decision and signals that the answer depends on how customers react to the higher rate.
coaching.model_approach_for_phase: Restate: 'We want to know whether raising the room rate from $160 to $180 increases profit, which depends on how our customers respond.' Then clarify.

phases.pass_criteria: Candidate restates the pricing decision and frames it around customer response.

phases.name: structuring
phases.interviewer_instructions: Ask how the candidate will decide. Look for: change in profit = change in revenue - change in cost, with revenue depending on occupancy (elasticity), extras, and any added room cost. Do not accept 'just raise it'.

coaching.explain: The clean structure is: new profit vs status quo. Revenue depends on how occupancy and extras respond to the higher rate; cost rises only if you must spend to justify the rate. So the crux is elasticity by customer type.
coaching.model_approach_for_phase: Lay out profit impact = change in revenue (occupancy x rate + extras) - change in cost, and pre-commit to analysing elasticity separately for business and tourist guests.

phases.pass_criteria: Candidate frames the decision as an incremental profit calculation driven by segment elasticity.

phases.name: analysis
phases.interviewer_instructions: When the candidate asks about customer types and who pays, release exhibit ex1_customer_mix. Guide them to test the $220 corporate cap and the business-centre lock-in for the 80% business segment, then the elastic 20% tourist segment.

coaching.explain: The insight is that 80% of demand is business travel billed to companies that allow up to $220 a night, and those guests are anchored by the business centre the nearby competitor lacks. So a move to $180 barely touches them. The elastic risk sits only in the 20% tourist segment.
coaching.model_approach_for_phase: Establish that business guests are inelastic up to $220 and sticky due to the business centre, so occupancy and extras hold for 80% of demand. Then isolate tourists as the only segment likely to drop.

phases.pass_criteria: Candidate isolates the inelastic business segment (with the $220 cap and business-centre lock-in) from the elastic tourist segment.

phases.name: synthesis
phases.interviewer_instructions: Ask for a recommendation. Look for: raise the rate, exploit the headroom to the cap, and handle tourists via segmentation rather than forgoing the increase. Reward naming a risk.

coaching.explain: A strong close raises the rate (business demand holds), notes headroom to push toward the $220 cap, and protects the tourist segment through price differentiation, e.g. 'executive' rooms for business at a higher rate and 'regular' rooms for tourists, rather than a blanket increase that risks tourist volume.
coaching.model_approach_for_phase: 'Raise the rate: 80% of demand is inelastic up to a $220 cap and anchored by our business centre, so $180 is safe and there is headroom toward $220. To protect the price-elastic 20% tourists, differentiate: an executive room for business guests and a regular room for tourists. Risk: if the competitor adds a comparable business centre, business stickiness weakens.'

phases.pass_criteria: Recommendation raises the rate, uses the cap headroom, and protects tourists via segmentation with a risk acknowledged.

common_errors: Confusing the rate change with the cap headroom
Dividing by the proposed rate instead of the current rate
Forgetting there is still headroom to the $220 cap after moving to $180

curveballs.injected_fact: Suppose the nearby competitor announces it is building a business centre of its own. Does your recommendation change? (Strong answer: business stickiness weakens, so lean harder on differentiation and service quality, and be more cautious about pushing toward the $220 cap.)

model_answer.framework: Incremental profit = change in revenue (occupancy x rate + extras) - change in cost. Revenue response is governed by price elasticity, which differs sharply by customer segment.
key_insights: 80% of demand is business travel billed to companies that permit up to $220 a night, so it is inelastic well past $180.
The business centre anchors corporate guests, who the $160 competitor cannot serve as well.
Only the 20% tourist segment is genuinely price-elastic and at risk from a blanket increase.
There is headroom of $40 between $180 and the $220 corporate cap to capture further.
model_answer.recommendation: Raise the rate. Business demand (80%) is inelastic to $220 and anchored by the business centre, so a move to $180 lifts revenue with negligible occupancy loss and room to push higher. Protect the elastic tourist 20% with price differentiation (executive vs regular rooms) rather than skipping the increase. Watch for the competitor closing the business-centre gap.
model_answer.walkthrough: Frame incremental profit, segment demand into business (80%, inelastic to the $220 cap, sticky on the business centre) and tourists (20%, elastic), conclude the increase is safe for business demand with headroom, and differentiate to shield tourists.

anchors.1: No structure; asserts 'raise it' or 'do not' without a profit or elasticity frame.
anchors.3: Frames incremental profit but does not split elasticity by customer type.
anchors.5: Frames incremental profit and pre-commits to analysing elasticity per segment.

anchors.1: Cannot compute the rate change or the headroom to the cap.
anchors.3: Computes the $20 increase but not the percentage change or the cap headroom.
anchors.5: Computes the increase, the 12.5% change, and the $40 headroom to the $220 cap.

anchors.1: Treats all customers as equally price-sensitive.
anchors.3: Recognises business inelasticity but overlooks the business-centre lock-in or the tourist risk.
anchors.5: Ties business inelasticity to who pays and the $220 cap, and isolates tourists as the only real risk.

anchors.1: Rambling or silent; does not explain why each question is asked.
anchors.3: Explains steps but does not narrate the segment-by-segment reasoning.
anchors.5: States priorities and walks through the elasticity logic per segment clearly.

anchors.1: No recommendation, or a blanket 'raise the price'.
anchors.3: Recommends the increase but omits the cap headroom or the tourist segmentation.
anchors.5: Raises the rate, exploits the cap headroom, differentiates to protect tourists, and names a risk.
